stances.claim: The most formidable challenge to federalism is the utter lack of time: Congress must pass the revision by March 13, 2019, but loses weeks to recesses, the budget, and political campaigning.
stances.rhetorical_move: timeline-arithmetic demolition of the 2019 ratification goal

stances.claim: Speaker Alvarez's election-cancellation proposal was 'the unthinkable' -- and the lawmakers' bonanza of indefinitely extended terms exposed the self-interest behind it.

The ConCom's bicameral American-model draft is substantially different from -- and in many ways contradictory to -- the PDP-Laban and House committee drafts, making unification within six months virtually impossible.

The ConCom's proposal of four separate high courts (each 'supreme in their own spheres') with a chief justice each is confusing and more characteristic of the Russian than the American system it claims to follow.
Splitting the impeachment power (Congress) from the trial/removal power (Constitutional and Administrative Courts) is another controversial design flaw.
Six months would be utterly insufficient to resolve all these problems for a Congress saddled with other vital work and members campaigning for political survival.

notable_anecdotes: Speaker Alvarez proposing the cancellation of the midterm election so lawmakers can focus on Cha-cha -- and the implicit benefit of extending their terms indefinitely without facing the electorate.

The 1986 Constitutional Commission (working full-time daily) taking about a year including ratification; the 2018 ConCom (also full-time daily) taking six months -- vs a Congress that cannot work full-time and needs four months for the budget alone.

The four-supreme-court design: Federal Supreme Court, Federal Constitutional Court, Federal Administrative Court, and Federal Electoral Court -- each with its own chief justice -- compared to the Russian system.
The split of impeachment (Joint Impeachment Committee of Congress) from trial and removal (Federal Constitutional Court and Federal Administrative Court) -- a constitutional anomaly.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban identifies the most formidable challenge to federalism as the sheer lack of time: the 1987 Constitution requires revisions to be approved by Congress and then ratified in a plebiscite held 60-90 days afterward, meaning Congress must pass the revision by March 13, 2019 to hit the May 13, 2019 midterm coincidence. Deducting the All Saints Day recess (two weeks), Christmas break (one month), and the four months typically consumed by the budget, Congress has only about six months -- and cannot work full-time daily as the 1986 Constitutional Commission (one year) and the 2018 ConCom (six months, both full-time) did. Speaker Alvarez's proposal to cancel the midterm election -- so lawmakers could focus on Cha-cha rather than campaign for 'political survival' -- was 'the unthinkable,' transparently offering legislators the bonanza of extending their terms indefinitely; Senate President Sotto initially agreed but reversed after reading the public mood, and Roque clarified the President wants the midterms held. Beyond timeline, the column identifies deep substantive conflicts among three versions: the ConCom's Bayanihan Constitution (bicameral, American model), the PDP-Laban concept (president as head of state for defense and foreign affairs; prime minister elected by the HOR as head of government), and the House committee draft (more French presidential-parliamentary with no VP). The ConCom also proposed four separate high courts -- Federal Supreme Court, Federal Constitutional Court, Federal Administrative Court, and Federal Electoral Court -- each 'supreme in their own spheres' with its own chief justice, a structure the author finds more Russian than American, plus a split between the impeachment power (Congress) and the trial/removal power (Constitutional and Administrative Courts). Six months would be utterly insufficient to resolve all of these problems, concludes Panganiban.
